## Summary

He's quitting the Whoop subscription after 18 months but keeping the hardware: the strap now runs **fully local on "zhoop" — his fork of "noop"** (an existing open project; relationship between noop and Whoop hardware not established at capture). No "fluff metrics," data stays on his phone. His one-line thesis: **"AI killed vendor lock-in."**

## Why it matters

- **First wearable data point in the vault.** Our fitness stack is still manual (Telegram-forwarded sessions; Strava/Strong import pending the user's go). This sketches a third path — local-first sensor data with AI doing the interpretation — that would sidestep both the subscription and the cloud-export problem when we get to that decision.
- **"AI killed vendor lock-in" is the load-bearing claim, and it's half true.** What actually killed it here: an open project (noop) that already did the hardware integration, plus a tinkerer willing to maintain a fork. AI lowered the *maintenance cost* of the fork. The lock-in wasn't the subscription — it was the effort wall. Worth tracking as a pattern; our own infra leans the same way (small dumb local processes over managed services).
- **"No fluff metrics" is a product-design claim, not just taste.** Whoop's recovery/strain scores are proprietary derivations; ditching them means either losing those signals or re-deriving them locally. The honest version of this note's skepticism: we don't know what zhoop actually computes.
- **Relevant to the Fitness Coach's future mandate** only as a design lens: when the user eventually chooses wearable tooling, "can we get raw data out" should be a first-class criterion, not an afterthought.
- **Skepticism gates:** screenshots not inspected; noop/zhoop unverified (no repo link in captured text); single-author claim with 299 replies of predictable tribe-war (self-host fans vs "just pay for the thing"); 18 months of his historical data — migrated or abandoned? — unknown. Capture-first, verify-later.
